chunk_findings.detail: The stamp-only step runs *after* `_close`, which is the function whose own docstring says it "end[s] the run's record: the upgrade itself when something was settled, else a failure." In exactly the case `_stamp_only` was added for — no results this run because every item is already acknowledged (so `ok` is empty) and the plan no longer lists anything — `_close` takes the `elif run:` branch and appends `run failed: "upgrade <frm> -> <to>: nothing settled"`. Only then does `_stamp_only` append a second, contradicting event `upgrade.applied {from: frm, to: to, target: to, categories: cats, items: []}`. Reproduce: project stamped 0.1.11 with 0.2.1 installed, all 0.2.1 items settled, run `ddflow upgrade --apply`; the committed log receives, for the same `run` id, a failed note followed by an applied event that advances the release to 0.2.1. Two problems follow from the ordering: (1) the run is recorded as failed even though the stamp was advanced, so any tooling/operator surface that resolves a run's outcome from `_close`'s note (the reason the `status: "done"`/`run` fields exist) reports the upgrade as unsuccessful; (2) the applied event is written with `run=""` (the call passes `""` for `run`), so it carries no `run`/`status` fields and cannot be attributed to the run that produced it. The stamp-only record should be written from inside/`_close`'s success path (or `_close`'s failure branch skipped when `_stamp_only` will advance), so a run is not simultaneously "failed" and "applied".

chunk_findings.detail: `settled_items` only credits a partial apply when the release it recorded as `target` is equal to the *current* `running` version. But `running` is the code version installed at the time `upgrade --plan` is executed, and a partial apply records whatever version was heading it at apply time (the diff's own comment says so: "an apply that recorded the release it headed for counts only when that is the running one"). Whenever the tool is upgraded between the partial apply and the next plan — exactly the environment described in the bug (project stamp 0.1.11, 0.2.1 installed) — the recorded target no longer equals `running`, so the record's acknowledged items are not added to `settled`, `config_items(changes, cfg)` re-emits them (changes for 0.2.0 are still `_wanted` because 0.2.0 <= running 0.2.1 and > baseline 0.1.11), and the plan is non-empty again. Concrete sequence: project stamp 0.1.11, ddflow 0.2.0 installed; `upgrade --apply` acknowledges the 0.2.0 config items, one item refused so the stamp stays 0.1.11, the record is written with `target="0.2.0"`, `from="0.1.11"`, `to="0.1.11"`; operator installs ddflow 0.2.1; `upgrade --plan` now calls `settled_items` with `running="0.2.1"`, the guard rejects the record because `"0.2.0" != "0.2.1"`, the acknowledged 0.2.0 items reappear in the plan, and the next `--apply` re-acknowledges them and appends another full batch to the committed event log — the "plan never empties / log grows every run" bug this change is supposed to fix. The id sets are the same config-item ids (config item ids are derived from the same `config_items` call), so filtering them by id would have been safe here; the target check is the only thing keeping them in the plan.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_stamp_only` provably cannot change the version the run reports, and its only observable effect is a second `_record` call for the same run. Walk the guard: it acts only when `not results and frm != to and not _unresolved(plan, set())`. The unchanged line immediately above it, `new_to = (frm or UNSTAMPED) if _unresolved(plan, ok) else to`, calls the same predicate on the same `plan` with `ok` (a superset of the empty ack set used by `_stamp_only`; when `results` is empty `ok` is empty too). If no item is unresolved with *no* acks, none is unresolved with `ok` either, so by the time `_stamp_only` runs, `new_to` is already `to` — the function returns `to`, i.e. exactly its input. In the other branch it returns its input verbatim. So `new_to = _stamp_only(...)` is a no-op assignment in every case, and the function's sole behaviour is the additional `_record(log, [], set(), frm, to, cats, backup_dir, reasons)`.

Concrete case: a project that was partially applied earlier (say the refused item was dropped and the rest were settled) so the now-filtered plan is empty while the stamp still lags — `frm="0.1.11"`, `to="0.2.1"`, `results=[]`. Line 341 sets `new_to="0.2.1"` and `_close(...)` (same `log`/`cats`/`backup_dir`/`reasons` parameter list as `_record`) records the `0.1.11 → 0.2.1` upgrade; `_stamp_only` then fires and calls `_record` a second time for the identical transition, so `ddflow upgrade --apply` still appends a duplicate upgrade event to the committed log on that invocation rather than being a no-op — the append-per-run behaviour the bug report complains about (log growing without new work) — and `settled_items` must then tolerate two stamp-moving events for one run. The docstring's claim that this function "moves the project to the release when the stamp still lags" is not met; the stamp move comes entirely from the pre-existing `_close` line.

data.decision: PROPOSED for the operator (nothing is built on it until accepted). (1) The global cap stays the HARD limit (the adaptive limit as today). (3) Capacity is held by a SLOT: an item lease already is one; a pipeline that has not claimed an item yet books one with ddflow slot book / ddflow_slot (owner, group, purpose), renews it (any call by the owner is an implicit keep-alive; explicit renew too), releases it, or it expires on a short default TTL judged lazily on read (no daemon), exactly as leases are; an expired slot stops counting at once and is reported by doctor/brief. data.alternatives: Per-vendor scripts (rejected: not shared, not testable); a daemon watching sessions (rejected: D-sched-no-daemon).
data.decision: PROPOSED for the operator; nothing is built on it until accepted. (1) ONE pure decision function (core/govern.py, the flowcontrol pattern) takes sampled meters (quota fraction per subject, context fraction per session, load) and the task's tier, and returns an action: continue | downshift(tier, effort) | checkpoint | compact | restart(on tier) | pause-and-ask | stop. Sampled at doors (hooks, statusline, ddflow calls, a cadence tick for headless lanes), no daemon (D-sched-no-daemon). (2) QUOTA LADDER on D-quotas, default marks: 40% cap new work at 'balanced' and medium effort; 60% cap at 'fast' for mechanical work and low effort otherwise; 80% pause-and-ask (D-quotas: refuse new work, pause in-progress items, resume at the reset or on 'quota continue'); each step has a hysteresis band and cooldown. (3) CONTEXT LADDER (per session): 60% plan a checkpoint; 75% write the handoff; 85% compact or restart at the next safe point (between gates, WIP committed); 95% emergency checkpoint. (4) FLOORS: a reviewer never drops below its configured tier or family (independence stays), a task tagged deep (architecture, security) is never downshifted; gate evidence rules do not change with the model. (5) TIER PREDICTION in three steps: a suggestion by the model at claim recorded with its rationale (bootstrap, followed only if the model is qualified and within the ladder cap), then a feature-based default (files and size, kind, severity, history), then calibration from the log (gate failures, rework, review findings, cost per tier) with escalation one tier up after repeated failures at a lower tier. (6) A model runs the ddflow loop only if QUALIFIED by a live smoke test of the rules (B-ac-smoke), recorded per model. (7) Applying a tier: dispatched subagents get the model at dispatch; a running interactive session cannot change its own model, so a step-down there is advice plus a restart on the lower tier with a handoff. **Where ddflow is wrong or outdated**
- **Cursor stop hook:** it can continue the agent. `stop` and `subagentStop` return `followup_message`, which auto-submits as the next message (`loop_limit` default 5, `null` is unlimited). `cursor.toml` treats `stop` as block-only.

**Kilo (CLI and VS Code share one engine)**
- Kilo 7.x is an opencode-v1 fork. The VS Code extension spawns `kilo serve`, so plugins and the SQLite session DB are identical on both surfaces.
- The plugin API has the hooks `chat.message`, `tool.execute.before/after`, `shell.env`, `experimental.session.compacting`, `experimental.chat.system.transform` and `event`. The `event` handler is called without being awaited, so it cannot block anything.
- Probe on 7.2.20 confirmed two things:
  - A thrown error in `tool.execute.before` blocks the tool, and the error text reaches the model.
  - A `session.idle` handler calling `client.session.promptAsync` starts a new turn. Kilo has no synchronous Stop hook, but this works as the equivalent of Claude's stop-and-continue.
- `promptAsync` also accepts `model`, `agent`, `system`, `tools` and `noReply`. That gives per-prompt model switching and a way to inject a session brief without a model reply.
- Kilo stops because the engine ends the loop when the model finishes without tool calls. Auto-approve only removes permission pauses.
- Kilo 7.6.0 added a built-in `/goal` loop, but the model decides when it is done. It does not exist in the installed 7.2.20.
- `kilo.db` holds sessions, messages, tokens, cost and model. `GET /event` is a server-sent-events stream with the same events a plugin sees.
- MCP: prompts become slash commands and roots are supported. Elicitation and sampling are not.
- Release cadence is several patch releases a week.

- **Qwen Code 0.25.1:** it has a Claude-style `Stop` hook with `decision:block` and a block cap of 8. The payload includes `context_usage` and `context_limit`, so the context meter is free. It also has `/goal` with an independent verifier, JSONL sessions, `qwen serve` and `-p` headless mode.

**1. The remote tools**
- **OpenClaw** is an MIT-licensed, self-hosted assistant built around a "Gateway". It is run by the OpenClaw Foundation (a 501(c)(3)), led by Peter Steinberger, with about 392k stars. It releases several times a day (v2026.10.2 and v2026.10.5-beta.2 both on 2026-10-12). Earlier names such as Clawdbot/Moltbot appear in press. The name may change again.
  - It has 20+ chat channels.
  - It is both an MCP server (`openclaw mcp serve`, stdio) and an MCP client with token/password/OAuth. Which outbound transports it speaks is UNKNOWN.
  - It runs coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI and others) through ACP via the `acpx` backend. Permission modes are approve-all, approve-reads or deny-all. Whether a harness permission prompt can be relayed to a chat user is UNKNOWN.
  - It has cron, a 30-minute heartbeat, and authenticated inbound hooks (`/hooks/agent`, `/hooks/wake`); the auth detail is UNKNOWN.
  - Its trust model is "one trust boundary per gateway", not hostile multi-tenant.
  - Its security record is poor, but I only have secondary press (341 of 2,857 ClawHub skills malicious; CVE-2026-25253). The NVD entry could not be verified.
- **Claude Code Remote Control** attaches the claude.ai web and mobile apps to a session running on your machine. The connection is outbound-only, uses short-lived scoped credentials, and needs a subscription login, not an API key. **Cloud sessions** run in a VM with a credential-injecting GitHub proxy.
- **ACP (Agent Client Protocol, used by Zed and OpenClaw)** is specified only over stdio. A remote HTTP transport is a draft. Don't confuse it with IBM's Agent Communication Protocol, which merged into A2A.
- **n8n** is an MCP client with bearer, header and OAuth2 auth. Its MCP server trigger speaks SSE and streamable HTTP, not stdio.
- **Hermes Agent** is MIT-licensed, has a messaging gateway and cron, and acts as an MCP client over stdio or HTTP.

**2. What ddflow already has** (read from the repo)
- The MCP server is a hand-written stdlib stdio server. It supports the legacy protocol revisions plus the stateless 2026-07-28 one. An HTTP transport via the `[mcp-sdk]` extra is planned but unused.
- There is no real authentication. "Operator-only" verbs are enforced by convention, for example D-reviewer-trust and `ddflow approve`. Nothing proves the caller is a person.
- The pieces to reuse are the event log with `wait`, leases, `jobs.py` (detached processes), `ticks.py` (periodic work inside any command), slots, and the governor decisions. The governor/quota code is decided but not built: `ddflow quota` does not exist in this checkout.
- Per D-sched-no-daemon, ddflow starts no agents today.
